info.name: SwitchYard Gateway
info.description:
Manual/automated coverage for everything SwitchYard supports through Phase 7 (Provider Abstraction, Core Proxy, Streaming Passthrough, Auth & Rate Limiting, Budget Enforcement & Admin API, Health Checking, Retry & Fallback Routing, Circuit Breaker): non-streaming and streaming /v1/chat/completions across all three configured providers, the request-validation error paths, streaming error semantics, the liveness/readiness probes on both listeners, the admin API for team/provider introspection and live limit/budget management, provider health, the fallback chain, and the circuit breaker with its chaos harness.

Authentication: the collection sends `Authorization: Bearer {{acme_key}}` on every request via collection-level auth. The admin listener has no auth of its own (Part 1 scopes auth to the public API), so the header is simply ignored there. Requests that must run as a different team override it per-request — see the Phase 6 folder.

Before running:
1. Start the gateway with real provider keys loaded (`GROQ_API_KEY`, `GEMINI_API_KEY` in `.env`) and Redis reachable — rate limiting and budget enforcement both depend on it.
2. Ollama requests need a local `ollama serve` with the configured model pulled (`ollama pull llama3.2:3b`) — otherwise skip that folder.
3. Adjust the `*_model` collection variables if your `configs/providers.yaml` lists different model names, and `team_id`/`*_key` if your `configs/teams.yaml` uses different IDs or keys.
4. The Phase 6 folder needs the gateway put into a deliberate failure state first; that folder's own description spells out the two setups.
5. The Phase 7 folder needs the gateway restarted with the chaos harness enabled and a few breaker thresholds lowered so the test runs in seconds rather than minutes; that folder's description gives the exact command. Unlike Phase 6 it needs no config-file edits and no provider stopped — the chaos endpoint puts the gateway into (and out of) its failure state.

Streaming requests: Postman buffers the full SSE body before showing it (it is not a progressive SSE viewer), so you will see every `data: ...` event at once in the response body. For a literal token-by-token demo, use `curl -N` instead — this collection is for correctness checks, not the visual demo.

Admin API requests target `{{admin_url}}` (port 9090), never `{{base_url}}` — the admin API is deliberately unreachable from the public listener. Running the "Patch Team" folder mutates the running gateway's in-memory team registry (not `configs/teams.yaml` on disk); the last request in that folder restores the original values so the collection is safe to re-run.

Re-reads configs/providers.yaml and configs/teams.yaml from disk, validates both fully, and only then atomically swaps them in — a valid reload here is what re-picks-up any hand edits made to either file since boot (including undoing a PATCH from the folder above, since a reload always reflects what's on disk, not prior runtime overrides). That path is covered by cmd/gateway's own `go test -race ./cmd/gateway/...` (TestReloadRejectedLeavesStoreOnOldConfig), which is safe to run because it never touches the real config files.

item.name: Retry & Fallback (Phase 6)
item.description:
Step 6.2–6.4 verification. Three of these need the gateway put into a specific failure state first; each request's own description says which.

SETUP A — "Ollama stopped": run `ollama stop llama3.2:3b` (or kill `ollama serve`). Wait for GET /admin/providers/health to show ollama `down` if you want to prove the chain *skips* it; run immediately if you want to prove the chain *retries then falls back off* it. Both are valid paths and the fallback header is `true` either way.

SETUP B — "Groq unreachable": in configs/providers.yaml change the groq entry's `base_url` to `http://127.0.0.1:9/v1`, then POST {{admin_url}}/admin/reload. Nothing restarts; the running gateway picks it up atomically. Undo by restoring the URL and reloading again.

With SETUP A and SETUP B both applied, the `fast` tier is: ollama (down) → groq (unreachable) → gemini (healthy). acme may use gemini and gets served; globex may not and gets a 503 that names only the two it was allowed to try. That single state is what proves both the fallback path and the allowlist-over-availability rule.

item.name: Fallback Headers on a Normal Request (no setup)

exec: pm.test("requested model header echoes what was asked for", () => pm.expect(requested).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get("groq_model")));
pm.test("fallback header says false, not absent", () => pm.expect(pm.response.headers.get("X-Switchyard-Fallback")).to.eql("false"));

request.description: The happy path, run with everything healthy. X-Switchyard-Fallback is explicitly "false" rather than omitted — a caller scripting against it should never have to read an absent header as a negative. Note the served model can differ from the requested one even here if the provider reports a dated model ID (e.g. ...-0125); that is not a fallback, which is why the boolean exists separately from comparing the two strings.

exec: pm.test("status is 200 — the chain found another option", () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
pm.test("requested model is the ollama one", () => pm.expect(pm.response.headers.get("X-Switchyard-Requested-Model")).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get("ollama_model")));
pm.test("served model is not the requested one", () => pm.expect(pm.response.headers.get("X-Switchyard-Served-Model")).to.not.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get("ollama_model")));
pm.test("not served by the stopped provider", () => pm.expect(pm.response.headers.get("X-Switchyard-Provider")).to.not.eql("ollama"));
pm.test("the response body is a real completion", () => pm.expect(body.choices[0].message.content).to.be.a("string").and.not.empty);

request.description: Needs SETUP A (Ollama stopped). The requested model's provider is gone, so the chain walks the rest of the `fast` tier and something else answers. Check the gateway log for the `falling back to next candidate` line — it names from/to, the attempts spent, the reason kind, and Step 6.4's estimated_cost_delta_micros.

item.name: Allowlist Beats Availability (SETUP A + B, globex)

exec: pm.test("status is 503 — the chain ran out of permitted options", () => pm.response.to.have.status(503));
pm.test("gemini is never attempted — globex may not use it, healthy or not", () => {
pm.test("every attempt says provider, model, attempt count and reason", () => {

request.description: Needs SETUP A + SETUP B, and authenticates as globex (whose configs/teams.yaml entry allows groq and ollama, never gemini). Both providers globex may use are broken; gemini is healthy and would have answered. It gets an error instead, and the breakdown proves gemini was never in the chain at all. Run the request below as acme against the identical gateway state to see gemini serve it — same failure, different team, different answer. That contrast is the whole compliance point.

item.name: Same State, Allowed Team Gets Served (SETUP A + B, acme)

exec: pm.test("served by gemini — the option globex was denied", () => pm.expect(pm.response.headers.get("X-Switchyard-Provider")).to.eql("gemini"));

request.description: Needs SETUP A + SETUP B, authenticated as acme. Identical request and identical gateway state as the globex one above — the only difference is the team's allowed_providers, and that alone decides whether this is a 200 or a 503.

item.name: Caller-Fault Error Is Not Failed Over (no setup)

exec: pm.test("error is the provider's own classification, not chain_exhausted", () => pm.expect(body.error.type).to.not.eql("chain_exhausted"));
pm.test("no per-candidate breakdown — the chain was never walked", () => pm.expect(body.error.switchyard_attempts).to.be.undefined);

request.description:
A max_tokens far beyond the model's ceiling is a request the provider will never accept. It is classified invalid_request, which is neither retryable nor fallback-eligible, so the caller gets the 4xx immediately instead of the same answer three providers and several round trips later. Confirm in the log that exactly one attempt was made and no `falling back` line was emitted.

Caveat: some providers clamp an oversized max_tokens instead of rejecting it. If this returns 200, that provider clamped — check the log for a single attempt rather than treating it as a gateway bug.

exec: pm.test("spend is recorded, not skipped because the model changed", () => pm.expect(body.spent_usd).to.be.a("number").and.to.be.above(0));

request.description: Step 6.4's billing check, run right after "Fast Tier Fallback". The requested model was Ollama's (free, $0.00 in configs/providers.yaml) and a paid provider actually served it — so a nonzero spend here proves the request was billed at the *served* model's price, not the requested one's. For a clean reading, POST /admin/teams/{{team_id}}/reset-budget first, then run the fallback request, then this.

item.name: Circuit Breaker & Chaos (Phase 7)
item.description:
Step 7.1–7.5 verification. Unlike the Phase 6 folder this needs no config edits and no provider stopped — the chaos endpoint puts the gateway into its failure state and takes it back out again.

SETUP — restart the gateway with the harness on and the breaker thresholds lowered so this runs in seconds:

  SWITCHYARD_ENV=dev \
  SWITCHYARD_CHAOS_ENABLED=true \
  SWITCHYARD_BREAKER_FAILURE_THRESHOLD=3 \
  SWITCHYARD_BREAKER_WINDOW=5m \
  SWITCHYARD_BREAKER_COOLDOWN_BASE=30s \
  SWITCHYARD_BREAKER_SUCCESS_THRESHOLD=1 \
  go run ./cmd/gateway

Window is stretched to 5m purely so you are not racing a 30s clock between manual sends; cooldown stays long enough to observe Open before it half-opens. Run the requests top to bottom — several depend on the state the previous one left behind.

WHAT THE CALLER SEES: breaking Groq's fast model does NOT produce errors at the client. The fast tier falls back to Gemini, so every request still returns 200 — that is the point of the whole phase. The breaker opening is visible in the response *headers*, in GET /admin/providers/health, and in the gateway log, not in a failed request.

NOT COVERED HERE: "exactly one probe in HalfOpen, others rejected" needs concurrent requests landing in the same instant, which Postman cannot express. That one is covered by `go test -race ./internal/resilience/...` (TestHalfOpenAdmitsOneProbeUnderConcurrency, 50 goroutines racing for one slot) and by TestReplicasShareOneProbeSlot for the cross-replica case.

item.name: 1. Chaos Refused Without Dev Flags (404) — run on a DEFAULT gateway

exec: pm.test("answers as though the route does not exist", () => pm.expect(body.error.type).to.eql("not_found"));
pm.test("body never admits a chaos harness exists", () => pm.expect(pm.response.text().toLowerCase()).to.not.include("chaos"));

request.description:
THE GUARD. Run this once against a gateway started normally (`go run ./cmd/gateway`, no SWITCHYARD_ENV, no SWITCHYARD_CHAOS_ENABLED) — then restart with the SETUP env above for every other request in this folder.

404 rather than 403 is deliberate: a 403 would confirm the endpoint exists and is merely refusing, which tells anyone probing a production gateway that the capability is there and worth attacking. A 404 is the same answer a build that never had chaos compiled in would give.

Also worth trying once: start with SWITCHYARD_CHAOS_ENABLED=true but WITHOUT SWITCHYARD_ENV=dev. Still 404, and the startup log carries `chaos harness was requested but refused: not a dev environment`. Both conditions are required, and neither is sufficient alone.

Confirms the SETUP env actually took. If this 404s, the gateway is not running with both SWITCHYARD_ENV=dev and SWITCHYARD_CHAOS_ENABLED=true — check the startup log for the `chaos harness is ENABLED` warning line.

exec: pm.test("message explains the rule must target something", () => pm.expect(body.error.message).to.include("must target a provider, a model, or both"));

request.description: A rule naming neither a provider nor a model would break every call the gateway makes. Even in dev that should not be reachable by fat-fingering one field, so it is rejected at validation.
The four valid modes are error, latency, rate_limit and drop. Rules are validated in full before any of them is stored, so a bad rule at the end of a list cannot leave half a rule set applied.

exec: pm.test("rule targets groq and the fast model only", () => {

request.description:
Targets ONE model on ONE provider, which is what makes request 8 (the sibling-model check) meaningful. Groq keeps serving its 120b model normally; only the fast model breaks.

The forged failure is a retryable KindServerError, so it exercises retry, then fallback, then the breaker — a non-retryable fault would exercise the give-up path and leave all three untested.

item.name: 6. Trip the Breaker — SEND THIS 3 TIMES

exec: pm.test("status is 200 — the caller never sees the broken provider", () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
pm.test("not served by the broken provider", () => pm.expect(pm.response.headers.get("X-Switchyard-Provider")).to.not.eql("groq"));
console.log(`served by ${pm.response.headers.get("X-Switchyard-Provider")} in ${pm.response.responseTime}ms — send this 3x total, then move to request 7`);

request.description:
PRESS SEND THREE TIMES (matching SWITCHYARD_BREAKER_FAILURE_THRESHOLD=3 from the SETUP).

Each send is exactly one failure against the groq+fast-model breaker — not one per retry. The breaker hears one verdict per candidate per request, because otherwise a single client request could contribute a whole threshold's worth of failures on its own.

Every send returns 200. That is the headline result of Phase 6 + 7 together: the primary is broken, the caller is unaffected. Watch the gateway log for the `falling back to next candidate` line on each send, and for `circuit breaker transition ... to=open reason=failure_threshold_exceeded` on the third — that log line is the "opens at the configured threshold, not before" checklist item.

On the 4th and later sends the log shows `skipping candidate on open circuit breaker` instead of a retry-then-fallback sequence: no provider call is made at all.

item.name: 7. Health Shows Groq Degraded by the Open Breaker

exec: pm.test("groq is degraded, never down — a breaker is a decision to stop trying, not proof of unreachability", () => pm.expect(groq.status).to.eql("degraded"));
pm.test("the transition reason names the breaker", () => {
pm.expect(groq.last_transition, "no transition recorded yet — wait one health-check interval (~30s) and resend").to.not.be.null;

request.description:
Step 7.4's health integration: the gateway is already refusing groq traffic, so reporting it healthy would contradict its own behaviour.

TIMING: health status is recomputed on the active checker's tick (default every 30s), NOT on the request path — that is what keeps Phase 5 inside the 10ms overhead budget. So there is up to a 30-second lag between the breaker opening and this endpoint saying so. If the test fails, wait and resend.

Degraded and never down is deliberate: escalating to down would drag /readyz through AllDown() on what may be a perfectly healthy fleet.

item.name: 8. Sibling Model Unaffected — RUN PROMPTLY AFTER 6

exec: pm.test("status is 200 — the sibling model still serves", () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
pm.test("a real completion came back, not a chain_exhausted 503", () => pm.expect(body.choices[0].message.content).to.be.a("string").and.not.empty);
pm.test("served by groq — direct proof the 120b breaker is closed while the 20b one is open", () => pm.expect(served).to.eql("groq"));

console.log(`served by ${served}, not groq — the health checker has already demoted groq to degraded, so it sank below gemini in the chain. Still correct (degraded sinks, it does not skip), but no longer isolating evidence. Re-run the whole folder and send this within ~30s of request 6 for the strict check.`);

request.description:
Step 7.4's granularity rule: the breaker is keyed on provider+model, so groq's 120b is untouched by the 20b breaker being open. Same provider instance, same API key, same base URL — only the model differs.

RUN THIS WITHIN ~30 SECONDS OF REQUEST 6 for the strict version. Here is the subtlety worth understanding: the *breaker* is per provider+model, but *health status* is per provider — so once the health checker notices the open breaker and marks groq degraded, groq's other models sink below healthy providers in chain ordering and gemini may serve this instead. That is correct behaviour (degraded sinks, it does not skip), but it stops being evidence of per-model isolation.

The unambiguous proof of isolation is TestBreakerIsPerProviderAndModelEndToEnd in internal/proxy, which uses one mock serving both models so anything keyed by provider alone would skip them together.

item.name: 9. Chaos - Swap to an 8s Latency Rule

exec: pm.test("the rule set was replaced, not appended to", () => pm.expect(body.rules).to.have.lengthOf(1));

request.description:
Sets up the next request. POST replaces the whole rule set rather than appending, so a demo script can put the gateway in a known state with one call instead of clearing first and hoping nothing was left behind.

Latency mode delays the call and then lets it proceed — it does not fail it. Groq would now take 8 seconds to answer this model *if it were called at all*. Request 10 proves it is not.

item.name: 10. Open Breaker Costs No Latency Penalty

exec: pm.test("returned in well under the 8s injected delay — the broken provider was never called", () => pm.expect(pm.response.responseTime).to.be.below(5000));
console.log(`${pm.response.responseTime}ms with an 8000ms fault armed on the primary — the open breaker skipped it without waiting`);

request.description:
THE POINT OF THE WHOLE PHASE, as a number you can read off the response.

An 8-second fault is armed on the primary. If the breaker were closed, this request would wait out that 8 seconds (times the retry count) before falling back. Because the breaker is open, the candidate is skipped before the budget check, before resolution, and before any provider call — so the request costs a cached state read instead.

That is the difference between a breaker and plain fallback: fallback alone still pays the full timeout on every request to a dead provider. Run this before request 12 (the reset) — afterwards the breaker is closed and this request really will take 8+ seconds, which is itself a useful contrast worth trying once.
Back to normal behaviour. The breaker is still open at this point — clearing the fault does not close the circuit, which is exactly why the manual reset below exists.

exec: pm.test("at least one breaker was reset", () => pm.expect(body.breakers_reset).to.be.above(0));

request.description:
Step 7.4's manual intervention: an operator who already knows a provider is healthy should not have to wait out a cooldown to prove it. Closes every breaker belonging to this provider and clears the shared Redis episode with it.

breakers_reset is the count actually touched, which is what distinguishes a provider name that matched nothing from one whose breakers were all already closed. Expect 1 or 2 here depending on whether request 8 caused groq's 120b breaker to be created.

If the shared Redis state cannot be cleared this returns 502 rather than 200 — the local breakers were still reset, but the rest of the fleet may be holding the old episode, and that is worth telling the operator rather than reporting a clean success.

item.name: 13. Groq Serves Normally After the Reset

exec: console.log(`served by ${served} — see this request's description if that is not groq`);

request.description:
The gateway is serving normally again with no chaos and no open breaker.

Do not assert on the provider here. Groq's *health status* is still degraded from the error rate the chaos run left in the passive window (last 100 requests or last 60s, whichever is shorter), so groq sinks below healthy gemini in chain ordering and gemini may well serve this. That is correct — degraded sinks, it does not skip — and it clears itself within about a minute.

The direct evidence that the reset worked is request 12's own breakers_reset count, plus GET /admin/providers/health returning groq to healthy once the window ages out.
"grok" instead of "groq". The name is validated against the configured provider list so a typo at incident time reads as an error rather than a silent no-op success.

item.name: 15. Breaker Route Does Not Shadow the Health Route

exec: pm.test("status is 200 — health still routes correctly", () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
pm.test("response is the health array, not a provider named 'health'", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json()).to.be.an("array"));

request.description: Mounting POST /admin/providers/{name}/breaker/reset puts a wildcard under /admin/providers, so the one routing hazard is "health" being read as a provider name. This confirms the literal route still wins.
